reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: NIST defines the recovery point objective (RPO) as the point in time to which data must be recovered after an outage. Here backups complete at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00, each is assumed to be restorable, and no other copy of the data exists.

Independent check: for periodic backups the worst-case loss equals the backup interval plus any delay before a backup becomes usable. With a 6-hour interval and no delay the bound is 6 hours, consistent with the 11:59 example.

Misconception to reject: 'the RPO is how quickly we restore.' Restore speed is governed by the RTO; the RPO concerns how old the recovered data may be. A fast restore of a 6-hour-old backup still misses a 1-hour RPO.
Change one factor: take snapshots every 30 minutes. The worst-case loss falls to 30 minutes, within the 1-hour RPO, provided each snapshot is complete and restorable.

Source and limits: the RPO definition follows NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.SP.800-34r1. A backup that fails a restore test provides no recovery point, so schedule restore tests as well as backups.

reasoningSteps: Use a synthetic schedule that creates instantaneous, complete and verified recovery points every 10 minutes: 10:00, 10:10 and 10:20. There is no replication lag in this simplified model.

reasoningSteps: Use a synthetic data history: a clean snapshot represents 11:30, a corrupting operation occurs at 11:45, and the error is discovered at 12:00. The live replica has already copied the corrupting operation.

Selective replay requires a justified consistency procedure and evidence separating valid from corrupt changes. Do not assume a newer timestamp or ordinary replication can undo logical corruption.

reasoningSteps: Use a synthetic outage lasting 30 minutes during which 120 work items per minute arrive and none are processed. After restoration, processing capacity is 180 items per minute while arrivals remain 120; all work is preserved.
The initial backlog is 30 x 120 = 3,600 items. Net drain after restoration is 180 - 120 = 60 items per minute.
Clearing the backlog takes 3,600 / 60 = 60 additional minutes, so full catch-up occurs 90 minutes after disruption.
Dividing by gross capacity gives 20 minutes but ignores ongoing arrivals. If capacity were only 120, the backlog would not drain under these steady assumptions.

System restoration and process catch-up are separate milestones. NIST notes that reprocessing time can matter to MTD; this fluid queue model is an original illustration, not a universal recovery forecast.
